newsitem.title: UK: EMU to remove foreign/local rating distinction - S&P.
newsitem.headline: EMU to remove foreign/local rating distinction - S&P.

text.p: Sovereign ratings for members of European economic and monetary union will no longer distinguish between local and foreign currency credit ratings after a single currency is introduced, a Standard & Poor's director said.

S&P public finance ratings director Konrad Reuss, speaking at a conference on EMU, also said that individual issuers of EMU member countries will no longer be limited by their country's sovereign ceilings as they are now.
This is because there will be an effective sovereign rating of triple-A assigned to EMU, Reuss added.
"It is not only a hypothetical concept, we will actually assign a triple-A rating to European Monetary Union."
EMU is due to start on January 1, 1999, with the creation of the European Central Bank (ECB) and the introduction of the euro single currency.
Current expectations are that it will initially include Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.
Reuss said under EMU, if a company or bank warrants a triple-A rating, then as part of a member country of EMU it can be rated higher than the country itself.
"The distinction between the local currency debt rating and the foreign currency debt rating will be history, and there will only be one rating," he said.
For example, Reuss said the Belgian government, whether it issued debt in dollars, yen, Swiss francs or the new euro single currency, will have one rating.
Under the new rating regime, he said, EMU member countries are most likely to receive their foreign currency ratings.
"The best proxy I can give you now for a country's rating under an EMU scenario would be its current foreign currency rating," he said.
"So you have a bit of a rating cliff for local currency bonds as the rating is likely to drop to the level of the foreign currency bonds."
Under this scenario countries such as Denmark, Finland, Ireland, Portugal and Sweden were likely to take on their lower foreign currency ratings than their local currency ratings.
